issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, sexual situations and being around children are hard-to-explain triggers in the absence of any related trauma content elsewhere in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on generic hyperarousal/dissociation and transportation-related cues, so these two triggers do not fit the trauma-specific pattern and weaken Triggers → Threat / Triggers → Memory coherence.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: Humiliation can occur after an MVC, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals otherwise suggest self-blame and social disconnection, yet no memory, threat, or trigger content reflects embarrassment, public exposure, disability, or shame-linked reminders. For this trauma type, permanent humiliation is insufficiently supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is poorly linked to the rest of the formulation. The profile’s active threat content is hyperarousal/startle and dissociative memory disturbance, and the selected strategies otherwise involve vigilance and situational avoidance. Undereating does not plausibly address any represented symptom cluster and feels disconnected from the threat/memory/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: 'Being around children' is a weak fit as a trauma trigger for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless the crash specifically involved children; nothing else in the profile supports children as a salient cue, so this trigger appears disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is possible but is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a motor vehicle collision. The accompanying appraisals are self-blame and alienation, but there are no other items suggesting shame/humiliation themes (e.g., social exposure, moral failure, visible disgrace), making this appraisal stand out as poorly integrated.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: 'Avoid open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on transportation cues, startle/physical threat reactions, and trauma memory phenomena from an MVC. Open-space avoidance suggests a different threat pattern (e.g., assault/agoraphobic vulnerability) that is not represented elsewhere.

A bicycle-specific trigger is difficult to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless the collision specifically involved a bicycle; the rest of the profile is vehicle/crash focused rather than bicycle focused, so this item stands out as trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: Alarm to unexpected touch suggests an interpersonal/assault-related threat cue more than a motor vehicle collision. In the context of the other threat items, generic startle and physical reactivity fit, but touch-specific alarm is not well linked to the reported trauma or the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is a broad social-identity appraisal that is not impossible, but it sits awkwardly with the otherwise self-blame/competence-focused appraisal pattern tied to an MVC. It is less clearly connected to the memory and trigger content than more trauma-specific appraisals would be.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not impossible, but here it is poorly supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links threat and appraisals to maladaptive strategies, and the other strategies are vehicle avoidance and thought monitoring, whereas undereating addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

vignette:
Frank is a sixty-seven-year-old widower, a retired military medic who spent thirty years treating battlefield trauma before the trauma found him on an ordinary highway. The collision happened just over fourteen months ago, on a rain-slicked evening in late October. He was driving home from a grocery run, stopped at a red light, when a pickup truck struck him from behind at nearly fifty miles per hour. The impact shunted his sedan into the intersection, where it was T-boned by an SUV. Frank remembers the sound of tearing metal and the smell of burned rubber and gasoline mixing with something else—a sharp, acrid odor he later identified as the deployed airbag’s chemical propellant. He remembers the silence afterward, and the way his hands, which had packed a thousand wounds, trembled uncontrollably as he tried to check his own pulse.

What he cannot do, even now, is tell the story in a straight line. When a therapist or a friend asks what happened, Frank finds himself losing the thread mid-sentence. He will start describing the rain, then suddenly he is talking about the smell, then he stops altogether because the sequence will not hold together in his mind. The memory feels alien to him, as though it belongs to someone else—a different Frank, a weaker Frank, a Frank who was not paying attention. Because that is the appraisal that has taken root: the event happened because of the way he acted. He should have seen the headlights in his rearview mirror. He should have tensed his body, braced for impact, done something. That he did not, that he was caught completely off guard, has become evidence of a deeper failing. He has come to believe he cannot trust himself to do the right thing. And if he cannot trust himself, he reasons, then he must be a weak person, all those years of composure in combat zones notwithstanding.

In the months following the crash, Frank developed a set of habits that have gradually narrowed his world. He stopped driving entirely, and he avoids being a passenger in any vehicle if he can help it. His daughter lives forty minutes away; he has not seen her since Christmas because he cannot bring himself to accept her offer of a ride. When he does have to go somewhere—a doctor’s appointment, a pharmacy run—he walks, even when the distance is impractical. The consequence has been a slow, grinding isolation. He used to volunteer twice a week at the VA hospital, a role that gave his retirement meaning. Now he stays home because the bus route passes the intersection where the crash occurred, and the thought of seeing that stretch of asphalt makes his chest seize.

The physical reactivity is relentless. Frank jumps at ordinary sounds—a car horn two blocks away, the hiss of a pressure cooker, the ding of his own microwave. His startle response is so hair-trigger that he has taken to sitting with his back to the wall in his own living room, scanning the window for movement he knows is not there. What frightens him most, though, is the thought monitoring. He has become vigilant toward his own mind, constantly checking whether he is thinking about the crash, whether he is about to think about it, whether a stray sensory cue will pull him under. He tries hard not to think about the trauma, but the effort itself feels like a trap: the more he suppresses, the more the memory intrudes. Sometimes the intrusion is auditory—he hears the screech of tires or the hollow thud of metal against metal, sounds that play inside his head with a vividness that terrifies him because they feel like proof that he is losing his grip.

The olfactory triggers are the hardest to manage. The smell of alcohol—beer on a stranger’s breath, hand sanitizer in a waiting room—sends him straight back to the scene, because the pickup driver had been drinking. Burnt smells, even something as benign as toast left too long in the toaster, activate the same cascade: racing heart, sweating, the conviction that something terrible is about to happen again. He has stopped cooking with oil. He has stopped going to restaurants where someone might order a beer.

What finally brought Frank to seek help was not the isolation or the startle responses, but a moment two weeks ago when he found himself standing in his kitchen, gripping the counter, unable to move because he had caught a whiff of something scorched from a neighbor’s barbecue. He stood there for ten minutes, frozen, waiting for the impact that never came. When he finally let go, his hands were shaking the way they had shaken in the car. He called the VA the next morning. He is afraid, now, that he is going crazy—that the thoughts he monitors so carefully will eventually take over entirely. But he is also, somewhere beneath the fear, hoping that someone can show him how to trust himself again.
